stops.name: Karlsbad, the secret flight before dawn
stops.campa: At three in the morning, telling almost no one, he slips out of the spa at Karlsbad in the post-chaise, under a false passport, calling himself Johann Philipp Möller, a merchant, then a painter. Overworked, stifled by office and by the long chaste bond with Frau von Stein, at thirty-seven he flees south toward the land his father's Roman engravings first opened to him as a child. It is the great rupture of his life: a rebirth deliberately sought. Italy, Italy, he has said, and now he goes.
stops.quote: Kennst du das Land, wo die Zitronen blühn?

stops.name: Verona and Vicenza, the amphitheatre and Palladio
stops.campa: At Verona he stands in the great Roman arena, the first antique monument he has seen entire, and marvels at how the oval mass gathers a people into one body. At Vicenza he walks among the buildings of Palladio and feels the man's godlike gift for making the ideal real in stone, harmony fixed in marble. The classical world he had known only from prints now rises around him solid and warm; he sketches, measures, and begins to see with a new, clear, southern eye.
stops.quote: Es ist etwas Wahres und Großes in dieser Kunst des Palladio, das sich nicht mit Worten aussprechen läßt.

stops.name: Venice, the sea-city and the gondola song
stops.campa: Venice, a thing built by human will out of the lagoon, delights and instructs him: the Piazza, the pictures of Veronese and Titian, the sea whose form he studies on the Lido, gathering shells and thinking of nature's law. At night he hears the boatmen sing the strophes of Tasso across the water, one answering another from far off, and is moved to tears by the folk-poetry still living in the people's mouth. He notes the crabs and the tides, the poet and the naturalist forever one man.

stops.name: Assisi, the Temple of Minerva
stops.campa: On the road to Rome he turns aside at Assisi, but not for the great basilicas of the saint, which he pointedly refuses to enter. He climbs instead to the little Roman temple of Minerva in the market-place, its Corinthian columns standing pure and whole from antiquity, and stands before it in reverence as before a first true classical building on Italian soil. The medieval and the Franciscan he passes by; it is the antique alone his converted eye now seeks. He walks back down happy.
stops.quote: Nun war ich endlich vor dem ersten vollständigen Denkmal des Altertums… ein so löbliches, dem Auge so wohltuendes Werk.

stops.name: Rome, arrival, and the being reborn
stops.campa: He enters Rome and is, he says, at last truly born. Lodging on the Corso with the painter Tischbein, still incognito, he walks among the ruins and the antiquities of the Vatican as through a country long dreamed. Here the fragments cohere; the ancient world becomes real to his eye; he sheds the northern gloom and finds the clear, plastic, classic seeing that will govern his art thereafter. The day I entered Rome, he writes, I count as my second birthday, a true new birth.
stops.quote: Ja, ich bin endlich in dieser Hauptstadt der Welt angelangt! … so kann ich sagen, daß ich erst von dem Tage an, da ich Rom betrat, ein neues Leben angefangen habe.

stops.name: Naples, the bay, the pleasure, the living folk
stops.campa: Naples astonishes him with its light, its swarming careless life, its blue bay under the smoking mountain. See Naples and die, runs the saying; here he throws off the last of his gravity and lets the sun, the sea, the fruit and the singing possess him. He climbs the streets among the lazzaroni and finds them not idle but happily alive. In this paradise, he says, one forgets oneself and the world, and I know not what to make of myself.
stops.quote: Von der Lage der Stadt und ihren Herrlichkeiten, die so oft beschrieben und belobt sind, kein Wort. 'Vedi Napoli e poi muori!' sagen sie hier.

stops.name: Vesuvius, the ascent to the crater's lip
stops.campa: Three times he climbs Vesuvius, the last time to the very rim while the mountain works. He stands amid the reek and thunder as it flings up glowing stones; a fresh eruption drives him back down the cinder slope in a rain of fire. Terror and delight together. The living volcano is nature caught in the act of creation and destruction, the primal fire under the classic calm: the very image his science seeks, forming and unforming without cease.

stops.name: Palermo, the public garden and the Urpflanze
stops.campa: Crossing to Sicily, in the public garden of Palermo among plants he had only known in tubs, now standing free and glad in the open air, the old question seizes him again: might one not find here, among this crowd, the Urpflanze: the archetypal plant, the one original form from which all the leaf-worlds of the earth unfold by metamorphosis? Everything, he sees, is leaf; and from that single insight the whole vegetable kingdom can be thought and even invented. It is the seed of his whole morphology.
stops.quote: Die Urpflanze wird das wunderlichste Geschöpf von der Welt … Mit diesem Modell und dem Schlüssel dazu kann man alsdann noch Pflanzen ins Unendliche erfinden.

stops.name: Rome, the second Roman year and the departure
stops.campa: Back in Rome he works with the artists, draws, studies the antique, completes Egmont and Iphigenie in their classic verse, and lives freely, at last, in the flesh as in the eye. When on the eve of Saint Peter's day he must go, he stands in the moonlit Colosseum and grieves as at a second death, murmuring lines of Ovid's exile. Twenty-one months of the fullest life close; he carries the south home in him for the forty years that remain.
stops.quote: Cum subit illius tristissima noctis imago, / Qua mihi supremum tempus in Urbe fuit …

stops.name: Weimar, Christiane Vulpius in the park
stops.campa: Home from Italy, restless and estranged from the pale renunciations of the past, on 12 July in the park on the Ilm a young woman of three-and-twenty, Christiane Vulpius, hands him a petition for her brother. She is a flower-maker, warm, unlettered, wholly of the earth. He takes her into his house without marriage, to the deep scandal of the court and the lasting hurt of Frau von Stein. The Roman Elegies pour out: pagan, sensuous, happy. This is his marriage in all but rite, and it endures.
stops.quote: Eine Welt zwar bist du, o Rom; doch ohne die Liebe / Wäre die Welt nicht die Welt, wäre denn Rom auch nicht Rom.

stops.name: Weimar, the birth of the son August
stops.campa: On Christmas Day Christiane bears him a son, Julius August Walther, the only one of their five children to live. Herder holds him at the font. Four more will come and die in infancy; this boy alone survives to grow, to serve the Duke, to marry the brilliant Ottilie, and, decades hence, to die before his father in Rome. The house on the Frauenplan now has an heir, born out of wedlock in the teeth of a scandalized town.

stops.name: Valmy, the cannonade and the new epoch
stops.campa: Dragged along as civilian guest of Karl August in the Prussian invasion of revolutionary France, he stands on the muddy field of Valmy in the autumn rain while the untried citizen-army holds firm under the cannonade and the disciplined kings' troops recoil. That evening, downcast officers ask the poet his thought. He rides forward under fire to feel the cannon-fever, and speaks the words that will ring down the centuries: here and today a new age of the world begins, and you may say you were there.
stops.quote: Von hier und heute geht eine neue Epoche der Weltgeschichte aus, und ihr könnt sagen, ihr seid dabei gewesen.
